newsitem.title: USA: COCOA - Analysts see U.S. Q3 grind up 3 to 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: COCOA - Analysts see U.S. Q3 grind up 3 to 10 pct.

text.p: Relatively low world prices, coupled with steady growth in consumer demand for chocolate, are expected to boost U.S. cocoa production rates in the third quarter of 1996, industry sources said.

U.S. cocoa grindings - a key barometer of consumption -- should rise between three and ten percent versus the same year-ago period, analysts and traders said, with the majority of forecasts falling toward the lower end of the range.
"Shipments have been good and I hear manufacturers are getting good orders," one analyst said. "But if it were above five percent, I would be surprised."
The data are slated for release Friday, October 18 at 0845 EDT/1245 GMT.
U.S. grindings in the third quarter of 1995 reached a record high of 94,485 tonnes, according to the Chocolate Manufacturers Association, a U.S. trade group.

But industry sources said they would also be watching for a downward revision to last year's third quarter grind figure. In reporting the 1995 second-quarter results, the CMA revised its year earlier figures by a hefty 10 percent.
The analysts' forecasts, which fall in line with a steady upward trend in cocoa consumption worldwide, come on the heels of surprisingly strong third-quarter output in Europe.
"This is a worldwide phenomena," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "I think it could be up 10 percent. Prices are cheap historically."

While many sources said the U.S. grindings were likely to echo the increased consumption patterns in Europe, no one expected the U.S. third quarter numbers to match the huge increases seen on the U.K. and Dutch grinds.

Dutch third quarter rose by 16.69 percent to 99,549 tonnes, while the U.K. grind shot up 42 percent in the third quarter to 48,855. Last quarter's the German grind rose a more modest seven percent on the year, to 65,824 tonnes, but still surpassed many analysts' growth expectations.
"We are not going to get the European increases," an analyst said. "They are helped by export demand and in the U.S. we do not export that much chocolate."
